title: Bind releases to signed approval
intent:
A caller could pass any revision to `release(revision)` and ship it without approval.

This PR adds signed approval to that decision. Follow the revision from the request to `ship(...)`, then see how the HTTP response and tests describe the outcome.

sections.title: The approval boundary
sections.overview:
**Before:** `requestedRevision → ship(requestedRevision)`. The caller chose what shipped.

**After:** `verifyApproval(approval)` runs first. An `Invalid` result returns `Rejected`; a `Valid` result allows execution to continue.

Two values now meet at this boundary: `requestedRevision` comes from the caller, while `verified.revision` comes from the signed approval. They are not interchangeable.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The signature proves which revision was approved. The code must also prove that it is the revision about to ship.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
Request[Caller revision + signed approval] --> Verify{Valid signature?}
Verify -- No --> Reject[Rejected result]
Verify -- Yes --> Ship[Ship caller revision]
Verify -. Signed revision is not compared .-> Gap[Issue 1]
```

**Review:** Follow the argument passed to `ship(...)`. Does it equal `verified.revision`?

diffs.summary: Call `verifyApproval(approval)` before `ship(requestedRevision)` and return `Rejected` for an invalid signature.

sections.title: What callers observe
sections.overview:
**Before:** a completed call returned `{ ok: true }`. **After:** the route sends the domain outcome, either `Released` or `Rejected`, in the response body.

The responsibilities stay separate. `release(...)` decides whether shipping is allowed; `postRelease(...)` translates that decision into HTTP. Other callers can reuse the domain rule without knowing about HTTP.

An invalid approval takes this path:

```text
verifyApproval → Invalid
release       → Rejected
Response.json → HTTP 200 + Rejected body
```

The last step is the mismatch. A client checking only `response.ok` sees success, even though nothing shipped.

**Review:** Check both the rejection body and the HTTP status. Issue 2 is anchored at the translation point.

diffs.summary: Serialize `Released | Rejected` with `Response.json(result)`; the status still needs an explicit mapping.

sections.title: What the tests prove
sections.overview:
The new tests cover signature rejection and a successful release. Read each fixture as a claim about the boundary:

- **Invalid signature:** expect `Rejected` and zero calls to `ship`.
- **Valid approval for A, request for A:** expect `ship("revision-a")`.
- **Valid approval for A, request for B:** not covered. This is the case that distinguishes signature validity from permission to ship.

The negative side-effect assertion matters. Checking only `result._tag` would miss a function that ships first and returns `Rejected` afterward.

**Review:** Add the A/B mismatch case and a route-level rejection test. Verify the result, HTTP status, and absence of shipping.

diffs.summary: Assert `Rejected` without shipping, then exercise a matching `revision-a` approval and request.
